title: Memory usage grows continuously and pods restart
description: Diagnose a memory leak that causes Kubernetes pods to restart by collecting heap dumps, analyzing GC patterns, and fixing the root cause in application code.

data.text: Your Kubernetes pods restart every few hours. The container memory limit is 512Mi, and the usage graph shows a steady climb from 200Mi to 490Mi before the OOMKill. CPU is normal, and there are no obvious traffic spikes. You need to find the memory leak, capture evidence, and fix it without increasing the memory limit.

items: Memory usage in Grafana or Prometheus climbs linearly and never drops after traffic decreases
Pods receive SIGKILL with reason OOMKilled in their status
Application logs show no errors before the kill
GC logs show decreasing time between full garbage collections
Heap size after GC is larger after each collection cycle
Restart count in Kubernetes increases steadily

terms.definition: Memory that is allocated but never released, often due to references that are never garbage collected.
Linux Out of Memory Killer terminates a process when the system or cgroup runs out of memory.
Automatic memory management that reclaims memory occupied by objects no longer in use.
A snapshot of the Java or .NET heap that shows which objects are consuming memory and what references them.
The state where available memory is low and the system is actively trying to free memory.

items: Confirm the leak: observe memory over time and verify it does not plateau
Check GC logs for shrinking free heap after each collection
Enable heap dump on OOM in your container runtime or application config
Analyze the heap dump with a profiler (dotMemory, Visual Studio Diagnostic Tools, or Eclipse MAT)
Identify the dominant object type and trace its references to find the root
Check for common leak patterns: event handlers, caches without eviction, static references

data.title: Event handler memory leak in .NET
data.content: Subscribing to events without unsubscribing prevents garbage collection of the subscriber:

data.caption: Memory leak lifecycle from allocation to OOMKill in Kubernetes
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Request allocates object] --> B[Object referenced by static cache]
    B --> C[GC runs but object survives]
    C --> D[Heap usage increases]
    D --> E[GC runs more frequently]
    E --> F[Heap after GC grows]
    F --> G[Memory approaches limit]
    G --> H[OOMKilled by Linux kernel]
    H --> I[Kubernetes restarts pod]
    I --> A

data.title: Heaps do not shrink automatically
data.text: In .NET and Java, the heap can grow to accommodate allocations but does not return memory to the OS eagerly. A plateau near the memory limit is a strong signal of a leak, not normal behavior.

data.title: Find a memory leak using a heap dump
data.description: Take a small application with an intentional memory leak. Generate a heap dump and analyze it to find the root cause.
steps: Create or clone a small API that leaks memory (e.g., by caching objects in a static list)
Run the app and generate load until memory usage climbs
Capture a heap dump using dotnet-dump or ProcDump
Analyze the dump with dotMemory or Visual Studio to find the leaking object type
Fix the leak and verify memory usage stabilizes
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to identify the exact object type and reference chain that is preventing garbage collection.

data.title: Summary
points: Verify the leak by observing memory growth over time
Collect a heap dump during the spike, not after the restart
Use a profiler to find the object type and reference chain causing the leak
Fix the root cause; do not just increase the memory limit
data.takeaway: Memory limits in Kubernetes are a safety net, not a target. If your app needs increasing memory over time, it has a leak.
